title: Rello creative test *autopsy*
dek: A buyer-inspectable example of how public product truth and live-ad evidence become a controlled creative test. No account access, invented performance data, or unapproved health claims.
lens: Meta creative strategy · sports nutrition · claim-safe spec work
sources: Rello site + Meta Ad Library + NSF + launch release

sections.heading: the *diagnosis*
sections.body:
Rello is qualified for a public-source specimen. The brand has a live DTC product, nationwide Sprouts availability, current NSF Certified for Sport listings for both bar flavors, and active Meta advertising.

The public opportunity is message expansion, not a claim that the current work is failing. Four active Rello ads found in the Meta Ad Library use the same primary text and near-identical lo-fi creator treatment. The current message compresses protein, creatine, clean ingredients, strength, recovery, energy, and everyday performance into one unit. This specimen isolates one sharper job: make creatine easier to remember by putting it inside a protein bar the buyer already carries.

items.label: PER BAR
items.note: Current product page and ad copy

items.label: NSF LISTED
items.note: Current NSF Certified for Sport listing

rows.claim: Rello has a live, purchasable protein-bar offer.
rows.evidence: Chocolate Crunch is listed at $53.99 for 12 bars. The page states 20g protein, 1.2g creatine, 9g fiber, and 260 calories per bar.

rows.claim: The strongest owned-message mechanism is reduced supplement friction.
rows.evidence: Rello says it started because nutrition should not feel like a second job and frames its products as a way to avoid powders, messy scoops, and separate products.

rows.claim: The product has current third-party sport certification evidence.
rows.evidence: NSF's listing, current September 2, 2026, includes Rello Chocolate Crunch and Vanilla Crisp protein bars under Certified for Sport.

rows.claim: Rello is actively advertising on Meta.
rows.evidence: The public Ad Library showed active Rello ads with Library IDs 1599041291569235, 3006942762998068, 2234300803807908, and 1593562705754643, started August 12-18, 2026.

rows.claim: The visible active sample concentrates on one creative pattern.
rows.evidence: All four observed ads repeat the same primary copy beginning with 20g protein plus 1.2g creatine and use approximately 41-43 second lo-fi creator videos. Public visibility does not reveal spend or results.

rows.claim: A narrower habit-friction message is a defensible next test.
rows.evidence: This is an inference from the repeated active copy and the brand's own origin language. It is not evidence that the current ads underperform.

sections.heading: two concepts worth *testing*
sections.dek: Concept A isolates the strongest owned mechanism. Concept B preserves the product's performance breadth but gives it a cleaner entry point.

items.why: Target: creatine-aware active professionals who buy powders but struggle with consistency. Tension: the ingredient is not the hard part; remembering another scoop is. Promise: protein plus 1.2g creatine in the bar already going into the bag. Proof: current label facts, portable format, NSF listing. Best first vessel: lo-fi creator/product demonstration.

items.action: B · The protein bar with a performance layer
items.why: Target: solution-aware protein-bar buyers comparing labels. Tension: most bars make protein the entire story. Promise: 20g protein plus creatine and fiber in one bar. Proof: product panel and ingredient list. Best first vessel: headliner static, then matched creator video if the message earns a second test.

blocks.label: Concept A · habit friction
blocks.text:
A1  If the hardest part of creatine is remembering the scoop, put it in the snack you already carry.

A2  My protein bar started replacing one more tub on the counter.

A3  20 grams of protein. 1.2 grams of creatine. No shaker bottle.

blocks.label: Concept B · product difference
blocks.text:
B1  Most protein bars stop at protein. This one adds 1.2 grams of creatine.

B2  The label is short. The job list is not.

B3  A performance bar for people who are done managing a supplement stack.

blocks.label: Lo-fi product demonstration
blocks.text:
OPEN · Show a creatine tub, shaker, and Rello bar on a kitchen counter.

VOICE: If your creatine routine keeps dying at the scoop, this is the idea behind Rello.

PROBLEM · Pack the tub away; put the bar in a work or gym bag.

VOICE: Another powder only helps if it survives your actual day. Rello puts 20 grams of protein and 1.2 grams of creatine into a bar you can carry.

PROOF · Tight shots of the wrapper and nutrition panel.

VOICE: The current bar also lists 9 grams of fiber, and both flavors appear in NSF's Certified for Sport directory.

BOUNDARY · Creator holds the bar; no body-transformation imagery.

VOICE: This is not a promise that one bar replaces every supplement or that one amount fits everyone. It is a simpler way to put creatine into an existing snack routine.

CTA · If the scoop is the step you keep skipping, read the label and see whether Rello fits your routine.

PRODUCTION NOTE · A creator may not present this as personal experience unless it is true and documented. Final spoken claims require brand approval.

blocks.label: 1:1 and 4:5 production specification
blocks.text:
GOAL · Make the format and mechanism legible in one second.

HEADLINE · The protein bar with creatine built in.

SUPPORT · 20g protein · 1.2g creatine · 9g fiber

PROOF CHIP · NSF Certified for Sport, only after the exact mark usage is approved.

VISUAL HIERARCHY · Headline first. Centered wrapper plus broken-open bar second. A shaker and scoop sit small and out of focus in the background as the displaced routine, never crossed out.

CTA · See the ingredients

DESIGN · High contrast, restrained palette taken from current Rello packaging, generous empty space, no athlete collage, no four-benefit icon cloud.

ONE-SECOND TEST · A stranger must be able to answer: this is a protein bar with creatine.

Hold back · strength gains, cognition, longevity, skin, gut, energy, recovery, cost savings, or replacement claims. Those would turn one test back into the current message pile.

sections.heading: the test *sequence*
sections.caption: Keep the message and vessel tests separate.

steps.title: 0 · Claim lock
steps.note: Brand approves the exact label facts, NSF mark usage, creator language, offer, and landing-page match before production.

steps.title: 1 · Hook test
steps.note: Keep the Concept A body, creator, edit, CTA, audience, and offer constant. Change only A1, A2, or A3.

steps.title: 2 · Read the signal
steps.note: The media buyer defines spend sufficiency and evaluates hold, click, conversion, and downstream quality. Public spec work supplies no threshold.

steps.title: 3 · Format swap
steps.note: Move the winning Concept A wording into the headliner static. This tests video versus static without changing the core message.

steps.title: 4 · Concept challenger
steps.note: Only after a usable vessel signal, introduce Concept B in the same winning format. Do not change concept and format together.

steps.title: 5 · Learning record
steps.note: Log what ran, spend, audience, dates, hook definition, conversion result, fatigue state, and the next decision.

sections.heading: strict proof *boundaries*
sections.body:
VERIFIED: current product facts, public brand language, current NSF listings, Sprouts availability, and the four active Meta ads observed.

LIKELY: a habit-friction message is underrepresented in the visible active sample and deserves a controlled test.

UNCONFIRMED: spend, CTR, hold rate, CPA, ROAS, audience breakdown, conversion volume, creative winner status, customer objections, creator rights, inventory depth, contribution margin, landing-page performance, and which claims Rello's reviewer has approved.

PROHIBITED INFERENCE: active does not mean winning; repeated copy does not mean fatigue; public-facing language does not prove customer demand. No concept launches until the client supplies account context, approved claims, production constraints, and an approval owner.
